# BPO: Staying Close to the Behavior LLM Creates Better Online LLM Alignment

Wenda Xu $^{1*}$ , Jiachen Li $^{1*}$ , William Yang Wang $^{1}$ , Lei Li

<sup>1</sup>UC Santa Barbara, <sup>2</sup>Carnegie Mellon University

$^{1}$ wendaxu, jiachen_li, william@cs.ucsb.edu, $^{2}$ leili@cs.cmu.edu

![](images/d998b1910c2d1930d59a92e7292fc724b5840b2886e7a0de3550c8bfdea0674f.jpg)

![](images/eb70c0f5ad380a660a22d0ef297c33c710e6a3d1313abd3cc7a19bc45a9ff885.jpg)  
Figure 1: Given the same annotation budget, our BPO (when $F = 2$ ) significantly outperforms offline DPO ( $F = 1$ ) on both TL;DR and Anthropic Helpfulness by introducing only one additional preference annotation phase. Its performance (when $F = 2$ ) even matches, if not exceeds, that of on-policy DPO ( $F = T$ ), which collects new annotations at every step.
